title: Embedded Finance & Banking-as-a-Service: FinTech's new business model
subtitle: How Grab and Shopee can lend money and sell insurance without a banking licence
openingQuestion: A ride-hailing app (not a bank) lets drivers draw wages early inside the app, and an e-commerce platform offers buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) right at the checkout page. What is the business model behind both features called?
openingOptions: Both companies obtained full banking licences of their own to provide financial services
Embedded Finance - a non-financial company embedding financial services in its core product
It is pure marketing; there is no real financial mechanism behind either feature
These companies are breaking the law by offering financial services unlicensed
explanation: Embedded Finance is the biggest trend in modern FinTech: rather than making the user leave a familiar app for a separate bank, financial services are embedded directly into the main product experience (ride-hailing, shopping, workforce management). BaaS (Banking-as-a-Service) is the infrastructure behind it: a licensed partner bank supplies banking APIs to the FinTech, the FinTech builds the user experience and owns the customer relationship, and the partner bank handles regulatory compliance, capital management and the core credit risk.

realWorldExample.company: Grab Financial Group and the super app model
realWorldExample.description: Grab expanded from a ride-hailing app into a financial super app: GrabPay (an e-wallet), GrabFinance (lending to drivers and partners), and micro-insurance - most of it built through partnerships with licensed banks and financial institutions in each country, rather than Grab obtaining full banking licences everywhere. It is the classic strategy for a technology company to move fast into financial services without carrying the capital and regulatory burden of a traditional bank.

quiz.question: In a BaaS (Banking-as-a-Service) model, who carries PRIMARY legal responsibility for banking compliance (KYC, anti-money-laundering, capital reserves) - the FinTech or the licensed partner bank?
options: The FinTech company running the app carries primary responsibility
The licensed partner bank carries primary responsibility
The regulator is responsible for supervising the whole flow
The two split responsibility in proportion to the revenue share
quiz.explanation: This is the core structure of BaaS: the partner bank - invisible as it is behind the FinTech's interface - remains the entity legally answerable to the regulator for the core banking obligations (KYC/AML, capital adequacy, protection of customer deposits). That is why BaaS banks run very thorough due diligence on a FinTech before partnering, since the partner's compliance failings can reach the bank's own licence. A regulator supervises rather than bears the obligation, and responsibility does not divide along a commercial revenue split.

quiz.question: Which factors do you need to analyse in the unit economics of a BNPL (buy-now-pay-later) product to judge whether the business model is sustainable?
options: Market share against domestic competitors on the same model
Total value of goods transacted through the platform each quarter
Revenue per transaction, cost of funds, and the bad debt rate
The number of newly registered users signing up each month
quiz.explanation: This is the lesson proven by a string of real failures across the global BNPL industry: impressive GMV growth can conceal weak unit economics - if the bad debt rate rises faster than the fee margin, the business is fundamentally buying growth by accepting a loss on every transaction, which cannot last however good the headline growth looks. Market share, transaction volume and sign-ups all measure size, and size is exactly what hides the problem here.

quiz.question: Why do many large traditional banks choose to partner with FinTechs through BaaS rather than treating them purely as competitors to be squeezed out?
options: It avoids having to invest in a new core technology stack
It shifts all the credit risk across to the FinTech partner
It cuts regulatory compliance costs to the bare minimum
It puts an existing licence to work reaching new customers
quiz.explanation: BaaS creates a genuinely strategic win-win: the partner bank earns infrastructure fees without carrying expensive marketing and customer acquisition costs, while reaching new customer segments through the FinTech's attractive product experience. That is why many large banks worldwide have built dedicated BaaS units, treating it as a new strategic revenue line rather than a defensive move. It does not remove the need for core technology investment, and it certainly does not lower compliance cost or offload credit risk - the licence stays with the bank.

quiz.question: In a BaaS model, who carries primary legal responsibility for compliance?
options: The partner bank, because the licence is in its name
The FinTech, because it owns the brand and customer experience
Split by revenue share between the two parties
The end user, because they sign the terms of use
quiz.explanation: The FinTech holds the interface and the brand, but the banking licence - and every AML, KYC and deposit protection obligation that comes with it - stays with the partner bank. That is why the bank has to supervise its FinTech partners closely: compliance risk cannot be outsourced. Owning the customer relationship confers commercial power, not legal liability, and a user accepting terms of use never assumes a regulated entity's duties.

quiz.question: Which factors have to go into the unit economics of a BNPL product?
options: Just the number of orders and the value of each one
Merchant fees, the bad debt rate and the cost of funds
App downloads and average time spent in the app
Market share against BNPL rivals in the same segment
quiz.explanation: BNPL charges the shopper no interest, so all the revenue comes from the discount the merchant pays, while the costs are the funding of the advance and the share of customers who fail to repay. The model only makes money when that fee exceeds those two combined - order growth on its own tells you nothing, and neither do downloads or engagement time, which measure attention rather than economics.

keyTakeaways: Embedded Finance: financial services built directly into a non-financial product (ride-hailing, e-commerce) instead of sending the user to a separate banking app

BaaS (Banking-as-a-Service): the licensed partner bank supplies the infrastructure and APIs, the FinTech owns the customer experience - and the bank still carries primary legal responsibility for compliance
The unit economics of an embedded financial product (BNPL, for instance) has to balance fee revenue, cost of funds and the bad debt rate - impressive GMV growth does not make a model sustainable
BaaS is a win-win: the bank reaches new customers through the FinTech's experience, the FinTech uses the bank's licence and infrastructure without obtaining one itself

practicePrompt.question: A FinTech startup announces that BNPL GMV grew 300% over the past year, but its gross margin fell from 3% to 1%. As a FinTech product finance professional, what should you ask to judge the real health of the business model?
options: GMV up 300% already proves the model works, and margins will improve on their own
Is the margin falling because bad debt is outrunning fee revenue, or because of new-market costs?
A 1% gross margin is the standard for the BNPL industry, so no further digging is needed
Margin does not matter at this stage; just concentrate on growing GMV further
practicePrompt.explanation: This is the core analytical skill of a FinTech product finance professional: telling 'deliberate investment in growth' (margin temporarily compressed by expansion costs, and recoverable) apart from 'unsustainable growth' (margin compressed because credit risk rose as the business pushed into weaker customer segments to hit a growth target). The two causes call for completely different management action.

summary.keyIdea: Embedded Finance and BaaS are the business models that let a non-financial company build financial services into its core product through a partnership with a licensed bank - a large growth opportunity that demands careful unit economics analysis so that phantom growth does not mask credit risk.
summary.commonMistake: Judging an embedded financial product on headline growth metrics alone (GMV, user numbers) without digging into the unit economics and the credit quality behind them
summary.action: When analysing an embedded finance product, always separate revenue and GMV growth from the real margin and the bad debt rate to judge whether it is genuinely sustainable

application.title: Applying it in FinTech product finance
application.message: Take an embedded finance product you have used yourself (BNPL, an e-wallet built into another app) and try to identify the partner bank or financial institution supplying the BaaS infrastructure behind it.
application.secondary: Analysing the unit economics of embedded financial products is one of the most sought-after skills right now as FinTech keeps extending the embedded model into new sectors.

sections.text: You no longer open a separate banking app to borrow money or buy insurance - financial services now hide inside the apps you already use every day. This is the Embedded Finance revolution.
Embedded Finance - finance disappearing into the product experience

Rather than finance being a separate destination (open a banking app, visit a branch), Embedded Finance builds financial services directly into the customer's journey through the main product: shopping and paying in instalments right at the checkout, a gig driver drawing wages early inside the shift management app, or a small business borrowing inside the sales platform it already runs on.

BaaS is the layered model that makes Embedded Finance work: a licensed partner bank exposes APIs that let a FinTech reach core banking functions (opening accounts, processing payments, extending credit) without the FinTech having to obtain a full banking licence itself - an expensive, multi-year, capital-heavy process. In return, the partner bank earns service fees and reaches new customer segments through the FinTech's product experience.
Unit economics - the real measure of health

The global BNPL industry has learned some expensive lessons: impressive GMV growth does not mean a sustainable business if the bad debt rate rises faster than the margin. A FinTech product finance professional needs to be fluent in unit economics: revenue per transaction, the cost of funds financing the advance, and above all the actual default rate among end users.

sections.title: The three layers of embedded finance
sections.subtitle: The user only ever sees the top layer, while the risk and the licence sit in the bottom one

concepts.def: Financial services disappearing into the main product - instalments right at the checkout, never leaving the app.
The API and operations layer connecting a non-financial business to a licensed bank.
The party holding the licence and bearing ultimate compliance responsibility - even though the user never sees its name.

sections.label: Worth remembering
sections.text: Unit economics is the measure, not user count. An embedded product can grow very fast and lose money on every transaction - and growth then simply makes the loss bigger.

lines: Embedded Finance is redrawing the whole boundary between a 'technology company' and a 'financial company' - understanding both the commercial opportunity and the financial risk behind the model is a core skill for anyone working in FinTech product finance.
The most important question is not 'how fast is it growing' but 'is that growth built on solid unit economics'.

diagram.label: A non-bank platform (ride-hailing, e-commerce) holds the customer base and the behavioural data
A licensed bank or institution supplies the infrastructure and the licence (BaaS)
Financial products embedded into the existing experience: pay later, lending, insurance
Revenue is shared between the platform and the licence holder
Measure real health by unit economics, not by user numbers
